Monitor your agents with signals

Evaluations overview
turns.first_useful_timing_reason: The observer may first capture progress. No reliable separate timestamp of first useful text is established.
turns.final_visible_text:
They form one loop. Tracing records what your app or agent actually does. Evaluations measure quality against fixed test cases before you ship. Signals score live agent traffic automatically, so problems in production show up. Weave describes itself as an observability and evaluation platform that helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and improve it over time [S5].

Tracing (the foundation): Traces capture each operation's inputs, outputs and structure as a Call (one recorded function or LLM call). They help you debug, evaluate and monitor LLM-powered code [S7]. There are two paths. Agent integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls and tool calls in the Agents view. LLM-application integrations capture individual Calls in the Traces view [S3].
Evaluations (testing before release): An Evaluation object combines a dataset of examples with one or more scoring functions (scorers, which grade outputs). You run it against a model or function, and each run measures performance [S2]. This lets you track which model and prompt versions produced which results, compare evaluations across metrics, and spot regressions [S2, S6].
Signals (monitoring in production): In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals can score response quality, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content, and they point you to the traces that need attention [S1]. A rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0; a tag is a label such as "user-frustration". Both are applied to matching spans (parts of a trace), and a turn is one exchange between the user and the agent [S4].

How they connect (my inference from the docs): traced agent conversations are what Signals score. The traces that Signals flag show where quality is slipping, which can guide new test cases and re-running evaluations as you change prompts or models. Weave also says you can score production traffic with the same scorers you use in evaluation [S9].

The difference is which version you get back. weave.ref("support_prompt:v3").get() loads version index v3, which is fixed. weave.ref("support_prompt").get() loads whatever version is currently :latest [S1]. Both short forms need weave.init(...). A fully qualified weave:/// URI doesn't [S1].

Key terms

A ref points to an object stored in Weave. Calling .get() fetches that object so your code can use it [S1].
Prompts are stored as versioned objects, so evaluations, experiments and production systems can point to the exact prompt version they ran with [S3]. Publishing a prompt with weave.publish creates a version that can't be changed [S1].

The two short forms

weave.ref(<name>) gets the :latest version. Every object has the :latest alias [S1, S2].
weave.ref(<name>:<alias_or_version>) gets a specific version. After the colon you can use an alias (like :production), a version hash or a version index (like v3) [S1, S2].
My inference: the result of support_prompt can change when you publish a new version, but support_prompt:v3 always gives the same version. Use the pinned form when you need results you can reproduce.

Do you need weave.init? Yes, for both short forms [S1]. A short ref like support_prompt doesn't say which team or project it belongs to, and weave.init supplies that.

import weave

weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")
pinned = weave.ref("support_prompt:v3").get()
latest = weave.ref("support_prompt").get()

Fully qualified URI Yes, it changes the requirement: weave.ref(<fully_qualified_ref_uri>) doesn't need weave.init(...) [S1]. The URI names the team, project, object and version itself [S2]:

import weave

prompt = weave.ref(
    "weave:///your-team-name/your-project-name/object/support_prompt:v3"
).get()

The version part of the URI works the same way as above: it can be a hash, an index like v3 or an alias like :latest [S2].

Pass two postprocessing hooks, postprocess_inputs and postprocess_output, to the @weave.op decorator. Weave changes the data it logs, and your function body stays exactly as it is. The docs give hiding sensitive data as an example use [S1].

postprocess_inputs receives a dict that maps each argument name to its value. It returns a new dict, and that dict is what gets logged [S1]. Use it to drop or mask the password argument.
postprocess_output receives whatever your function returns and gives back a transformed version for the trace. For example, it can return a copy of your object with private fields replaced by "REDACTED" [S1].
Your function still gets the real password, as shown in the example where func uses hide_me to build its result [S1].

Things to keep in mind:

This only works in Python. The docs say it isn't available in TypeScript yet [S1].
I'm assuming the function returns the real object to whoever calls it, since the output hook is described as changing logged data. The docs don't say this outright.

turns.final_visible_text:
To evaluate an agent, trace it with Weave's Agents (conversation) workflow, write an LLM-judge scorer, then run every task in your dataset through weave.EvaluationLogger. You judge the agent's whole trajectory, meaning its turns, tool calls and results, because you can't grade an agent by string-matching one output [S1].

Prerequisites: a CoreWeave Forge account, Python 3.10+, pip install weave anthropic, and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set in your environment. That setup applies if Anthropic is both your agent model and your judge, as in the docs [S3].

Steps

Initialize and trace. Call weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]"). Then wrap each agent run in start_conversation(...), which contains turns, model calls (turn.start_llm) and tool calls (turn.start_tool). If you instrument by hand like this, turn off implicit patching. Otherwise, each conversation gets traced twice. If you use a framework integration (Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents), leave patching on and skip the manual start_* calls [S4].
Define a dataset. Write a list of tasks, each with a user_request and success_criteria [S2].
Write the judge. A scorer is any plain function. In the example, it prompts a judge model with the request, the success criteria and a plain-text transcript, and returns {"passed": bool, "reason": str} [S2].
Run and log the evaluation:
ev = weave.EvaluationLogger(name="support-agent-eval", model="v1", dataset="support-refund-tasks")

for task in tasks:
    with ev.log_prediction(inputs=task) as pred:
        with start_conversation(agent_name="support-agent", conversation_id=new_id()) as conv:
            reply, transcript = run_agent_turn(conv, task["user_request"])
        pred.output = reply
        pred.log_score("task_completion", judge_task_completion(task, transcript))

ev.log_summary()

Run the agent inside log_prediction so its traced conversation is linked to that row of the evaluation. In this snippet, run_agent_turn, new_id and judge_task_completion are placeholders for your own code [S2, S4].

Review the results. In the Evals tab, open your run. The Call tab shows each task's passed verdict. View spans opens the linked traces [S2].
Compare versions. Re-run with a new model label (for example "v2") and compare the scores, latency and cost [S5].

turns.final_visible_text:
Since you call Anthropic directly and have no framework, instrument the loop by hand with Weave's agent tracing helpers. Each piece of your loop maps to one helper: the session is a conversation, each user request is a turn, each messages.create call is an LLM span, and each tool you run is a tool span. A span is one timed step in the trace. [S1, S2]

How to set it up

Turn off autopatching. When you call weave.init, pass settings={"implicitly_patch_integrations": False}. Otherwise Weave also logs each Anthropic call on its own, and every model call appears twice. [S1]
Nest the spans. start_conversation groups turns. start_turn creates an invoke_agent span, start_llm creates a chat span, and start_tool creates an execute_tool span. In Python, all of these work as with blocks, which close the span and save its data even if an exception is raised. [S2]
One span per step. Open a separate start_llm for every model call in the loop, and a start_tool for every tool call the model asks for. On LLM spans, use record(...) to save token usage, the response ID and the model name. On tool spans, set tool.result. [S1, S4]
Keep your own message history. You still have to send tool results back to Claude yourself, as the docs' loop does. [S4] Tracing only groups the spans; it doesn't give the model any memory.
import json
import anthropic
import weave

weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]",
           settings={"implicitly_patch_integrations": False})
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MODEL = "[YOUR-CLAUDE-MODEL]"
TOOLS = []  # your Anthropic tool schemas

def run_tool(name, args):
    return "[YOUR TOOL RESULT]"

def run_turn(history, user_message):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_message})
    with weave.start_turn(user_message=user_message, model=MODEL):
        while True:
            with weave.start_llm(model=MODEL, provider_name="anthropic") as llm:
                resp = client.messages.create(
                    model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, messages=history, tools=TOOLS)
                text = "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
                llm.output(text)
                llm.record(
                    usage=weave.Usage(input_tokens=resp.usage.input_tokens,
                                      output_tokens=resp.usage.output_tokens),
                    response_id=resp.id, response_model=resp.model)
            history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
            tool_uses = [b for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
            if not tool_uses:
                return text
            results = []
            for b in tool_uses:
                with weave.start_tool(name=b.name, arguments=json.dumps(b.input),
                                      tool_call_id=b.id) as tool:
                    tool.result = run_tool(b.name, b.input)
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id,
                                "content": tool.result})
            history.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

with weave.start_conversation(agent_name="[YOUR-AGENT-NAME]"):
    history = []
    print(run_turn(history, "[USER QUESTION]"))

The Weave calls follow the docs. [S1, S4] The Anthropic parts (tool_use and tool_result blocks, the while loop) are my adaptation of the docs' OpenAI example, and I haven't run this code. When it runs, each turn should appear in the Agents view with its model calls and tool calls nested inside it. [S1]

Inside each start_llm span, call llm.record(...) with a weave.Usage object and response_model=resp.model. Weave works out cost from two things: complete token usage and a model ID it can price. If either is wrong or missing, the trace shows 0 in / 0 out or Cost -, even when everything else looks correct. [S5]

What to record

input_tokens must be the total input, including cached tokens. Weave prices cache reads and cache writes at their own rates and subtracts them from the input total. [S5]
Anthropic counts cached tokens separately. It reports cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens outside input_tokens, so add them back in to get the total. Then also pass both cache fields to weave.Usage. If you leave them out, usage and cost can show as roughly zero, because cached tokens are often most of the input. [S5]
output_tokens: pass it as Anthropic reports it. [S5] weave.Usage also has a reasoning_tokens field. [S6]
Model ID: Weave uses response_model first and falls back to the model you passed to start_llm. A short alias such as sonnet can't be priced, so pass the exact model ID from resp.model. [S5]
record(...) only sets the fields you pass. [S5]

In the earlier loop, replace the llm.record(...) call inside with weave.start_llm(...) as llm: with this (the same pattern as the docs' Anthropic example): [S5]

u = resp.usage
llm.record(
    usage=weave.Usage(
        input_tokens=u.input_tokens
        + u.cache_read_input_tokens
        + u.cache_creation_input_tokens,
        output_tokens=u.output_tokens,
        cache_read_input_tokens=u.cache_read_input_tokens,
        cache_creation_input_tokens=u.cache_creation_input_tokens,
    ),
    response_id=resp.id,
    response_model=resp.model,
)

Do this on every chat span, which means every model call in the loop, so each one carries its own usage and model ID. [S5] One caution: I haven't run this code, and the docs don't say whether Anthropic ever returns None for the cache fields. If you see a TypeError when adding them, use (u.cache_read_input_tokens or 0) and the same for the creation field.

I can't give you an exact call for weave.enable_hallucination_free_mode(). I couldn't find that function in the Weave docs I searched, and nothing I read promises an agent will never hallucinate. Writing that call would mean inventing an API.

What the docs do describe are scorers: checks that look at your app's output and flag possible hallucinations after it's been generated. They help you measure and catch problems, but they don't stop the model from hallucinating.

HallucinationFreeScorer (built in): checks whether your AI system's output includes hallucinations based on the input data. You can change its system_prompt and user_prompt to define what "hallucination" means for you. Its score method expects an input column named context, and you can use column_map if your data uses a different name. In the documented example it runs inside a weave.Evaluation and reports has_hallucination counts [S1].
WeaveHallucinationScorerV1 (local scorer, Python SDK only): a small model that runs on your machine and returns a result with a passed flag and metadata [S2].
import weave
from weave.scorers import WeaveHallucinationScorerV1

hallucination_scorer = WeaveHallucinationScorerV1()

result = hallucination_scorer.score(
    query="[USER_QUERY]",
    context="[RETRIEVED_CONTEXT]",
    output="[AGENT_OUTPUT]",
)
print(f"Output is hallucinated: {not result.passed}")

This follows the documented example [S2]. You could check result.passed at runtime and return a fallback answer when it's False. That's my suggestion, not a documented feature. It lowers the risk of hallucinations but doesn't eliminate them, because the scorer itself can be wrong.

In short, tracing records what your application or agent does. Evaluations test it against a fixed set of examples so you can compare versions. Signals score real agent conversations in production. Each one answers a different question.

Tracing (records what happens): There are two ways to trace. Agent integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls and tool calls from multi-turn agents, and show them in the Agents view. LLM-application integrations record individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave Calls in the Traces view [S3].
Evaluations (offline testing): An Evaluation object brings together a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions (scorers). You run it against a model or function. Each .evaluate() call creates an evaluation run, which you can compare with other runs to spot regressions. Think of the Evaluation as a blueprint and each run as one measurement [S2].
Signals (production monitoring for agents): The Signals tab in the Agents view shows tags and ratings on your agent's conversations. Tags are labels like "user-frustration" or "nsfw". Ratings are numeric scores from 0.0 to 1.0. Both are assigned to matching spans. A turn is one exchange between the user and the agent [S4]. Signals can automatically score response quality, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content. They point you to the traces that need attention [S1].

How they fit together (my inference from the docs):

Trace your agent first. Signals work on the conversations shown in the Agents view, and agent tracing is what puts them there [S1, S3].
Before shipping changes, run evaluations to measure them against fixed test examples and catch regressions [S2].
Once the agent is in production, use Signals to catch quality and safety problems, then open the flagged traces to see what went wrong [S1].
